Know Your Rights: Trump’s Birthright Citizenship Executive Order
July 31, 2025 Guides & Reports
On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order to limit birthright citizenship.

On the same day, the Asian Law Caucus, with our partners, the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of New Hampshire, ACLU of Maine, ACLU of Massachusetts, NAACP Legal Defense Fund and State Democracy Defenders Fund, filed a lawsuit in New Hampshire challenging the executive order.
Other groups and state governments have filed similar lawsuits in multiple states.
The cases, including ours, secured preliminary injunctions that block the Trump administration from implementing its executive order.
On June 27, 2025, however, the Supreme Court issued a decision in _Trump v.
CASA,_ limiting the nationwide effect of those injunctions.
In response to the Supreme Court decision, ALC, together with our partners, filed a nationwide class-action lawsuit,_Barbara v.
Our case challenges the Trump administration’s executive order, in order to fill the gaps in coverage left by the _CASA_ decision.

**On July 10, 2025, the federal judge in our class-action lawsuit****issued a preliminary injunction****to again block the executive order from going into effect for**_**all**_**children affected by the executive order nationwide.**Meanwhile, executive departments have begun to publish guidelines on how they would implement Trump’s executive order in the event it takes effect.
These guidelines are not law and cannot be implemented because there are nationwide preliminary injunctions blocking the executive order.
This resource addresses questions about the executive order’s implications and potential impacts.

If you are concerned that your child might be impacted by Trump’s executive order and would like to speak with the Asian Law Caucus, please provide your contact information and someone from ALC will follow up with you directly.
You can also join our Equal Under the Law campaign to defend our freedoms by sharing your story.

### Recent Developments
What is the class action case Barbara v.
Trump about?
Who does it cover?
_Barbara v.

Trump_ is a class-action case filed by ALC and our partners that seeks to strike down the Trump administration’s executive order on birthright citizenship and permanently stop the administration from applying it to anyone.
We filed the case on June 27, 2025 to address the gaps in protection from the executive order that were left by the Supreme Court’s decision in _Trump v.

The _Barbara_ case covers a nationwide class of all children affected by the executive order, which means any child born in the United States on or after February 20, 2025, whose parents are neither a U.S. citizen nor a lawful permanent resident at the time of the child’s birth.

On July 10, 2025, the judge in our _Barbara_ case issued a preliminary order blocking the administration from applying the executive order to any child in the class, while the court considers the legal challenge to the lawfulness of the executive order.

This injunction applies to all affected children,no matter the state in which they are born, and regardless of whether their parents are involved in any other pre-existing case challenging the executive order.
What was the Supreme Court Trump v.
CASA decision about?
On June 27, 2025, the Supreme Court issued a decision in _Trump v.
CASA_, which concerned three consolidated cases brought by individuals, community organizations, and 22 states challenging the constitutionality of Trump’s executive order on birthright citizenship.

In all three cases, the lower courts had previously issued preliminary orders referred to as “universal injunctions” which had preliminarily blocked implementation of the executive order, while the cases proceeded, not just for the parties in the cases, but for all affected people nationwide.

The Trump administration petitioned the Supreme Court to put those nationwide injunctions on hold, arguing that the injunctions should apply only to the identified plaintiffs, not as to people and states who are not part of those cases.

In its June 27 decision, the Supreme Court agreed with the Trump administration and held that federal trial courts do not have the authority to issue “universal injunctions” to cover people who are not part of the case.

The court found that the block on the executive order in the three cases therefore applies only to the plaintiffs and states involved in the three cases, and sent the cases back to the trial courts to decide whether or not a broader injunction is necessary to provide the states involved in those legal cases with “complete relief.”
The Supreme Court did _not_ address the underlying question of whether Trump’s executive order is constitutional or not.
That ultimate question is still pending in the lower courts.
Is there any gap in protection for children born in states that have not challenged the executive order because of the Supreme Court’s CASA decision?
There is no gap in protection for children born in states that have not challenged the executive order.

Though the Supreme Court in _CASA_ narrowed the nationwide injunctions blocking the birthright executive order to just the parties involved in the cases before it, the Supreme Court held that the executive order was not to go into effect for 30 days after its June 27 ruling.
Before that 30 day period expired, several federal courts issued new orders that continue to block the executive order from being implemented nationwide.
*   The judge in the _Barbara v.
Trump_ case issued an order on July 10, 2025 that blocks the executive order from being applied to a nationwide class of all affected children.
The injunction in _Barbara_ protects all affected children, regardless of the state where they were born or their families’ involvement in an existing lawsuit.
*   On July 24, 2025, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, in _Washington v.
Trump_, upheld the nationwide scope of a district court injunction barring implementation of the executive order, notwithstanding the Supreme Court’s CASA decision.

In doing so, the Ninth Circuit reasoned that a nationwide injunction is needed to provide the state plaintiffs with “complete relief” because any implementation of the executive order, even as to other states, will result in a loss of funding, added costs, and serious administrative upheaval due to the new systems the states would need to create to determine US citizenship and eligibility for federal benefits that the states administer.
*   On July 25, 2025, the district court judge in _New Jersey v.
Trump_ reaffirmed his preliminary injunction barring the executive order from taking effect nationwide based on similar grounds.
What does the Supreme Court’s CASA decision mean for “universal” or “nationwide” injunctions going forward?
The Supreme Court’s decision to curtail federal trial courts’ authority to issue national injunctions is a devastating development.
The decision limits the ability of impacted people to efficiently secure emergency protection at a time of unprecedented attacks on the constitutional rights of people across the country.

Nationwide injunctions are important to create uniformity so that our constitutional rights do not differ based on where in the U.S. we live or whether or not we have the means to sue to vindicate our rights.
Without a nationwide block of unconstitutional executive orders, the protection of essential freedoms requires piecemeal lawsuits that are cumbersome and impractical.
A nationwide injunction may still be achieved through a class-action lawsuit with a nationwide class.
These tend to be more complex and difficult to secure on an emergency basis.
### Trump's Birthright Citizenship Executive Order
What is birthright citizenship?
Birthright citizenship refers to the legal principle that someone born in a country is automatically a citizen of that country, regardless of their parents’ citizenship status.
The United States is one of over 30 countries with birthright citizenship.
Birthright citizenship is a constitutional right guaranteed by the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.
If you are born in the United States, you are a citizen.
What does President Trump’s executive order say about birthright citizenship?
As written, the executive order attempts to get rid of birthright citizenship for U.S.-born children of certain immigrants, born after February 19, 2025.
Specifically, it says the federal government will no longer consider U.S.-born children to be citizens if neither parent has citizenship or permanent immigration status.
Who does the executive order apply to?
In July 2025, the Trump administration released more details on how it would implement the executive order.

If it were to go into effect at a date yet to be determined, it would apply to any child born in the United States whose father is not a U.S. citizen or legal permanent resident, and whose mother is in the U.S. without legal status or in the U.S. on a “lawful but temporary” basis. “Lawful but temporary” status includes, but is not limited to, mothers with:
*   Humanitarian visas and pending applications, including pending applications for U-visas, T-visas, and asylum
*   Temporary protected status (TPS) and humanitarian parole
*   Deferred Action for Childhood Arrival (DACA) recipients

*   Student, work and family visas, such as H-1B (specialty occupation workers), H-4 (dependents of H-1B), H2-a (temporary agricultural workers), F-1 (students), J-1 (exchange visitors), L-1 (intra-company transferees), L-2 (dependents of L-1), O-1 (extraordinary ability), and P-1 (athletes and entertainers)
*   Tourist visas, such as B-1 (business visitors) and B-2 (tourists).
A child stripped of U.S. citizenship under this executive order would be denied their rights as a U.S. citizen.
The child will not be able to obtain a Social Security card or U.S. passport.
The child’s access to critical federal programs like CHIP, SNAP and Medicaid will be jeopardized.
Unless they find another way to get immigration status as they grow up, they will be barred from voting, jury service and holding certain jobs.
What if one parent is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident?

If the executive order goes into effect, children born in the U.S. to at least one parent who is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident would still be a U.S. citizen, regardless of the other parent's immigration status.
Would the executive order affect mothers who have asylee or refugee status?
The executive order does not explicitly address children whose mothers have asylee or refugee status, and whose fathers are neither U.S. citizens or legal permanent residents.
The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) did, however, address this in a July 25, 2025 memo.

According to USCIS, people granted asylum and refugee status are “lawful and not temporary.” Therefore, according to USCIS, the executive order should not apply to mothers with asylum or refugee status.
It is important to note, however, that the July 25 USCIS is not law, and is intended only as an indication for what the agency would do in the event that the executive order takes effect.
When does the executive order take effect?
As written, the executive order states that it is to take effect after February 19, 2025.
However, because of injunctions issued by multiple lower courts applicable to all affected US-born babies across the country, that effective date is no longer applicable.
The government may appeal those injunctions.
We will continue to update this website for developments.
What would ending birthright citizenship mean for people in this country?
Ending birthright citizenship would not only impact immigrant communities, but every American.
The harms and disadvantages of any implementation are clear and unavoidable:

*   **Ending birthright citizenship would mean government intrusion during childbirth.** Currently, all children born in the U.S. can apply to get their social security number without any investigation into their parents’ immigration status.
The executive order may change that.
It could turn doctors and hospitals into immigration agents, and launch investigations into the lives of every new parent and newborn.
*   **Trump’s policy would be costly to parents and all taxpayers.**The American Immigration Council (AIC) points out that ending birthright citizenship would be extremely costly and time consuming.

The U.S. government would have to create a large new bureaucracy responsible for determining the citizenship of all children born in the U.S. State governments, who are tasked with recording the birth of children and then reporting that to the Social Security office, would incur significant costs from developing new systems to verify children’s citizenship status.A study from the National Foundation for American Policy estimated that ending birthright citizenship would cost parents $600 in government fees to prove the citizenship status of each baby, and likely an additional $600 to $1,000 in legal fees.
*   **Trump’s policy would complicate the way U.S. citizens prove their status.**A U.S. birth certificate is typically sufficient to prove U.S. citizenship, but this executive order may change that.
Citizen verification may be replaced with a burdensome process of having to trace one’s family heritage and produce documentation of ancestral relations.

*   **Ending birthright citizenship means changing the status of certain infants from U.S. citizens to undocumented immigrants.**Children affected by this order face risks of health and economic instability as they would be ineligible for basic benefits through federal programs like CHIP, SNAP and Medicaid.
And without citizenship, their immigration status would be uncertain, which would cause a state of fear and uncertainty that can be very damaging for children.
If children are denied U.S. citizenship because of Trump’s executive order, could they get citizenship from their birth parents’ home country?

If the order goes into effect, whether impacted children could get citizenship from their parents’ home country would depend on different factors, including, but not limited to, their parents’ immigration status, home country, and whether the U.S. has diplomatic relations with their parents’ home country.
Without birthright citizenship, some children could be left stateless, without any country recognizing them as a national or a citizen.
If not by an executive order, are there other ways that politicians can get rid of birthright citizenship?
Although Congress may try to change federal laws protecting birthright citizenship, birthright citizenship is also enshrined in the Fourteenth Amendment.
Any attempt to take it away would require changing or amending the U.S. Constitution.
Changing the U.S. Constitution requires two thirds of both the House and the Senate.
Additionally, 3/4 of the nation's state legislatures would need to ratify any change.
What can I do to fight back against this illegal and inhumane order?

If you are an individual who may be directly impacted by Trump’s executive order, or if you would like to learn about how you can support the campaign to protect birthright citizenship, please contact the Asian Law Caucus through this form.
Sharing resources and knowledge with your family, friends and networks is one of the most powerful things we can do in the face of Trump’s agenda of chaos, fear, and division.
Remind them that birthright citizenship is a constitutional right!
Feel free to share the information on this page, and other resources listed below from ALC and our trusted community partners.
We must continue to advocate for what our families, neighbors and communities really need.
President Trump and his billionaire backers are pursuing a reckless attack on our freedoms instead of solving the problems that would create safer communities and brighter economic futures.
People who have work or student visas or who came to the U.S. as refugees and asylum seekers are also aspiring citizens.
But the immigration system moves slowly, and people must overcome tremendous hurdles that take years and years, if it ever works.

Most Americans believe that we should have an immigration system that is rooted in our values and that helps people put down roots and thrive - and in the face of these unconstitutional attacks, we can join together to fight for what our communities truly need.
